speechtext:
Yes; and now that the
hon. member has asked that question I may quote from both. I have been quoting from the majority report but there was also a report submitted by the minority. Let me read further, however, from the same report:
We do not consider that inquiry should be ordered where associations merely complain that rates are too high or unfair, or where, owing to a temporary rate war, rates from a foreign country may have been lower for a short time than from the United Kingdom.
That is rather a strange doctrine in view of what my hon. friends have been saying. However, the point I want to emphasize-and I do not wish to be misunderstood or misquoted-is that in this very intricate and complex question, which has been investigated by the very best authorities on the subject for many years, it is recognized that the difficulties being as involved as they are, it is
Ocean Shipping Rates

undesirable to seek to straighten them out by any arbitrary act of parliament. A course must be followed which will tend to promote harmonious relations between shipper and ship owner.
Now, my hon. friend suggests that there may be a minority report. There was. Let me state that the main portion of this report deals with the subject of rebates rather than conferences, although the two are reported on together. This is an extract from the minority report:
We who sign this minority report think that, before the adoption of legislation declaring illegal the deferred rebate system, or involving great interference by a government department with the details of the working of a highly complex industry, and leading probably to much litigation, a real attempt should be made to give effect to a system of conciliation and limited supervision by the board of trade.
There again you have the same doctrine expounded. I shall not weary the House by quoting further from that report. I read this, however, for the purpose of impressing upon the members of the House this fact: It is true this is a complex and delicate question, fraught with the greatest difficulties, and in spite of all the experience we have behind us there is a grave danger in injecting into it arbitrary legislative action.
My hon. friend referred also to the report of the agricultural committee of two years ago. He said that it was one of great importance. If that is the case, why did not the government some time within the last two years take cognizance of this clause in the agricultural committee's report, which report was commended to the House by the minister this afternoon:
The committee desire to bring the facts in this regard to the earnest attention of the House,-
Dealing now with the North Atlantic conference.
-and would respectfully suggest that the Minister of Railways and Canals should take the matter up with those responsible for the management of the boats of the Canadian Government Merchant Marine, so that the complicity of the Canadian Government Merchant Marine in this combine may be brought to an end immediately.
This afternoon the minister professed to have a great regard for this report; but for two years since the report was made the Canadian Government Merchant Marine has been "sitting in" in this conference. I am not blaming the management for that, I am merely stating the fact. For two years the government have gone sweetly along their way ignoring this report, and now they come forward to tell us that it is of great importance and is in support of the report made by Mr. Preston, and that therefore his report should be accepted by the House.

My hon. friend also addressed to the House as a reason for the recognition of the Preston report and its acceptance certain quotations from the evidence taken by the Dominions Royal Commission. Does he not recall that his quotations refer exclusively to New Zealand! and to trade to British ports- British trade? I am going to deal with that at some length in a moment or two. What I want to point out to my hon. friend is that he is justified in quoting the Dominions Royal Commission in regard to grievances that New Zealand1 or some British ports had, but he is not justified in expending nearly a million and a half dollars of the taxpayers money to subsidize the Petersen interests.
Now, I address myself directly to the resolution. Its basis will be found in a section of the Speech from the Throne which I desire to quote in laying the foundation for my argument, and the House will bear with me a moment while I again bring to their attention this paragraph from the Governor General's speech:
It is becoming increasingly evident, however, that quite as important a factor as the customs tariff in their effect upon production and living cost9 are transportation coats and rates, by land and sea. It is the opinion of my advisers-
The government.
-that the attention of parliament at the present session should be directed more particularly to the desirability of effecting a freer movement of commodities through an equalization of railway freight rates as between provinces and localities, and through a lowering of carrying charges upon shipments by water of the products of the farm, the mine, the forest, the fisheries, and of our manufacturing industries.
Some measure of control of transportation by land and sea is obviously essential-
And so forth. In other words, Mr. Speaker, we have presented to us by this official document these suggestions:	First, that the government have in mind the freer movement of commodities; and, secondly, the lowering of the carrying charges.	And it alleges that
there is a powerful steamship combine restraining the export trade. The very essence of the proposal embodied in the resolution now before the House rests on this test: Will the proposal bring about the control of ocean freight rates?	That, I say, is the
test of the whole question and I purpose focusing the attention of the House upon it. Will the proposal of the government bring about a freer movement of commodities and a lowering of carrying charges? Or perhaps I should be more charitable and say:	Is it
likely to bring about this result? Is it reasonable to expect that it will? What is the basis of the proposal? It is found in a report by one, W. T. R. Preston. His report

Ocean Shipping Rates
is offered as the reason for the resolution and for the remedy suggested, and it is all the evidence adduced by the government to support the charge that a combine in restraint of trade exists. I wish to call the attention of the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) and of the Minister of Trade and Commerce to the fact that when this resolution was originally placed on the order paper I asked for the correspondence between Mr. Preston and those affected, or for any correspondence bearing upon the subject. The hon. Minister of Railways (Mr. Graham), who replied, stated that there was no correspondence so far as he knew. So we have only this report to support the contentions of the government that such a combine exists.
Now, Mr. Speaker, our business as a House is to analyze and weigh this proposal. I ask, first: Does it offer a satisfactory remedy of the alleged grievance? Secondly: Has the maker of this report demonstrated that the alleged injury is an actual injury? These are the two questions I ask at the moment, and I purpose examining the report in regard thereto. All through the report the maker of it refers to the North Atlantic conference a3 a combine in such terms and in such a tone as to convey the impression that it is an evil and sinister thing. I apprehend. Sir, that it is not the part of an impartial investigator to adopt at the outset and to preserve throughout his report to the end a prejudiced attitude towards the subject of his investigation. The least that such an individual should do is to seek to be fair and impartial in his investigation. I am not for the moment suggesting that there is not a combine, but I say that the maker of the report is not justified in starting from the premises that an evil and sinister influence exists in the form of a combine.
In the second place, I want to say this: A combination of trade interests is not necessarily in itself an evil thing, and I think the House ought to pause and consider that. The Prime Minister is very fond of pausing this session, and I invite him to pause for a moment and consider this point, that a combination of trade interests, I do not care what they are, is not necessarily an evil thing.

subtopic: AGREEMENT WITH SIR WILLIAM PETERSEN- MOTION IN FAVOUR OF RATIFICATION
speechtext:
My right hon. friend
says, "hear,, hear," and I know that that is sound. Then I say to him that this report bears evidence that this institution referred to is judged and condemned from the very commencement and before any investigation was held. Indeed, the minister (Mr. Low) this afternoon referred to the fact that ever
since last June he had had in his mind this ten-ship remedy for the situation. Now let me proceed. A combination of interests, or a conference, or whatever you like to term it, a combine, if you will,-although I do not like to apply the word combine because almost invariably it carries with it a suggestion that is not necessarily contained in the word, but a combination of interests in regard to shipping-may have some beneficial results.
I say it may have. It may stabilize service; it may result in a uniformity of rates; it may improve shipping conditions; it may render possible recovery of losses in shipping; it may fix regularity of service. These are some of the things it may do, and are these evils? Everyone within hearing of my voice knows they are not. As a matter of fact, Mr. Speaker, no one disputes the fact that there is a conference, or a combination of interests existing in connection with shipping. It is unnecessary to establish that; it is admitted. The point we have to decide, however, is this: Has this conference been conducted contrary to the interests of the public? Has it been injurious? Has it been sinister? Or, on the other hand, has it contributed to the benefit of the country and to the benefit of shipping? I think we must admit that there are some benefits accrue from this conference, and I wish to state them. I think it is necessary and only fair to do so if we want to be impartial in this matter.
I know as a matter of my own personal knowledge, and I think it will not be disputed, that about the beginning of the year, about March, which is the beginning of the shipping season on the St. Lawrence, and the same thing applies to other sections, a list is supplied freely to shippers giving the fixed sailing dates of ships throughout the whole season from March, in the case of the St. Lawrence, to October or November. Now these fixed sailing dates are very valuable to shippers. They enable shippers to contract for the future: shippers are thereby enabled to provide for the contracting of delivery of goods to other countries for months ahead; they are likewise able to contract months ahead for the purchase and receipt of goods from other countries. Furthermore, by this method of fixed sailings the shippers, large and small, are assured of cargo space. In addition to that, there are almost daily sailings fixed from the port of Montreal. The reason I take the port of Montreal is this: There is no doubt in my mind from reading the resolution and the report that the point of attack-shall I say?- is the St. Lawrence route, or the port of Montreal and the lines running from there. In a

lesser degree, of course, other points will be affected. Now I submit, Mr. Speaker, that these are things that are beneficial to the shipper in this country; these are things that we ought to recognize and frankly acknowledge.
I turn now to the consideration of another British report, which I have under my hand. It is the report of the Commission on "Shipping and Shipbuilding, a commission appointed, I think, by Mr. Asquith in 1916. The commission reported in 1918, a very excellent report, comprising a large volume, and most exhaustive in its research and in its findings. I want to read an extract from that report to form the basis of some further comments. This report, mark you, is dealing with the question of conferences, with the question of this great combination of conferences, if you like, referred to in the report of Mr. Preston:
Conference Agreements. Broadly, conference agreements are designed to prevent the kind of abuses which has attracted so much attention in the New Zealand trade hut immunity from such abuse may be bought at too high a price. Shipping, however, could not subsist on rate wars, and the whole object of conferences is to avert them and to produce equality of rates and stable conditions in the great ocean trades. This aspect of the matter was clearly brought out in the report of the Royal Commission on Shipping Rings-
That is the report to which the minister referred, and which I have also under mv hand:
-and we see no reason to dissent from the general conclusions stated in that report.
Let me pause to point this out. Through all the reports of these British investigating commissions, the report of 1909, the report of 1918, the Imperial Shipping committee's report, the report indeed of the Dominions Royal Commission, there runs a singularly uniform note, that it is inadvisable to precipitate conditions that bring about rate wars, and inadvisable also to have too much government interference with shipping and with the operation of ships on the high seas. I sav this is singular, and it is rather important and most interesting.
Now in connection with the report that we have as a basis for this resolution there is a letter issued by the party who prepared this report, Mr. Preston. He says:
I acted on my own judgment, and so forth.
I thought it better to have a frank discussion and I therefore present d the following memorandum.
I have under my hand the memorandum which he prepared, and which he suggests in the report that he sent to all the shipping concerns. I do not know whether they received it, but I notice in the press of this

morning or yesterday that one after the other of the shipping companies have absolutely denied ever having received any invitation from him at all; but whether they received it or not does not alter the fact I wish to place before the House. What I wish to point out is the strange procedure followed by this gentleman. He pre-judges the case. If you will read the letter-I do not intend to read it all-you will find he declares that a combine that is sinister in its influence exists. Mark you, Mr. Speaker, this letter is supposed to be addressed to individuals whom he declares he is going to invite to a discussion; but before he invites them, indeed, in the very letter he alleges to have sent them as an invitation, he tells them that they are in an evil combine, a combine of sinister influence. He furthermore tells them, and this is the strangest feature, that a decision had already been arrived at. He tells them that it was proposed to deal with the matter in one of two ways:
(1)	By an arrangement with an independent steamship company with government assistance, and government control over freight rates or,
(2)	The establishment of a government service between British and Canadian ports with modern vessels.
The former is regarded as the more desirable.
So he had already judged, before he made any steps to inquire into the business at all, what course he was going to pursue. Then in the latter part of the memorandum he indulges in what is undoubtedly a threat. For instance, he tells the shipping interests in connection with this company which he proposes to establish that:
The government railways traverse the Dominion of Canada in about 2-1,000 miles of tracks or service. It is fair to presume that whatever action the government takes in the matter, will be towards linking up the suggested ocean transportation with this enormous mileage of National railwaysand so on. In other words he simply says this:	You ship owners and shipping companies are leagued together in a combine and I judge you and condemn you. That is his first point. Secondly he says:	I have
already found a remedy and that remedy is the organization of a separate company-in this case the Petersen Company under government subsidy. In the third place he says: It is my intention, and it is the government's intention, to link this special company, subsidized by the government, up with the railways; and the inference is left, to the prejudice of all other concerns as far as the securing of freight by these railways is concerned.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: AGREEMENT WITH SIR WILLIAM PETERSEN- MOTION IN FAVOUR OF RATIFICATION
speechtext:
Was not Mr. Preston, in the statement which he made,

basing his remarks upon the finding of a committee of this House, to the effect that there was a North Atlantic combine?

subtopic: AGREEMENT WITH SIR WILLIAM PETERSEN- MOTION IN FAVOUR OF RATIFICATION
speechtext:
Well, I have already referred to that. The Prime Minister, I think, perhaps is right; but let me put to him the question I put to the minister; I am glad to put it to him because he is the leader of the government:	If this finding of the committee
on agriculture of two years ago is of such importance, why did the government not take cognizance of this clause which I read a moment ago and which I will read again:
The committee desire to bring the facts in this regard to the earnest attention of the House, and to respectfully suggest that the Minister of Railways and Canals should take up the matter with those respons'ble for the management of the boats, so that the complicity of the Canadian Government Merchant Marine in this combine may be brought to an end immediately.
Now, I ask the Prime Minister this question: If that report is of such grave importance as he would suggest, why did not the government two years ago pull the Canadian Merchant Marine out of the combine? If the existence of a combine, to which the right hon. Prime Minister now refers, was established by that committee to a sufficient extent to form the basis of Mr. Preston's report so that he need investigate no further, why did the government allow its own ships to continue for two years in that iniquitous combine?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: AGREEMENT WITH SIR WILLIAM PETERSEN- MOTION IN FAVOUR OF RATIFICATION
speechtext: I am told that the ships that were built as part of the merchant marine were not at all suited for the class of transport that is required between here and the Old Country. The matter was looked into, it was gone into very carefully at the time, and when the government found that the merchant marine were not suited in any way to meet the situation that we are face to face with, we began to take other means to bring about an effective meeting of the situation.

subtopic: AGREEMENT WITH SIR WILLIAM PETERSEN- MOTION IN FAVOUR OF RATIFICATION
speechtext:
My right hon. friend will
pardon me, I do not wish to be impertinent, but he has not answered the point at all.

subtopic: AGREEMENT WITH SIR WILLIAM PETERSEN- MOTION IN FAVOUR OF RATIFICATION
speechtext: Oh, oh.

subtopic: AGREEMENT WITH SIR WILLIAM PETERSEN- MOTION IN FAVOUR OF RATIFICATION
speechtext:
Some one laughs. I will
deal with the question of the suitability of the ships in a moment, I have the necessary memoranda under my hand. I am now dealing with-the propriety shall I say-? of government ships continuing for two years in a combine that is declared by the government's own emissaries to be an evil thing, continuing for two years after a committee had reported
Ocean Shipping Rates
-and upon this report they rest their case,- that the combine existed.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: AGREEMENT WITH SIR WILLIAM PETERSEN- MOTION IN FAVOUR OF RATIFICATION
speechtext:
I am told-I
speak subject to correction-that one of the operations of this combine is, that if any line withdraws from it it will immediately attempt to undertake to put that line completely out of business. Now the merchant marine was in bad enough state when this government had to take it over, and we were not looking for a means to utterly destroy its usefulness.

subtopic: AGREEMENT WITH SIR WILLIAM PETERSEN- MOTION IN FAVOUR OF RATIFICATION
speechtext:
I really have too high a
regard for the Prime Minister to attribute that to him, as a serious observation and the ground for my hesitancy will be disclosed before I finish my remarks to-night. I am not going to be driven away from this point: The fact remains that it is alleged that the combine existed. The government takes in perfect faith the report of the committee on Agriculture of two years ago-I do not, but the government does-they take it to the extent of saying that Mr. Preston was warranted in accepting the report holus bolus without any further investigation. And yet they come before this House and say in the words of the Prime Minister "We had to keep our ships in this evil combine for two years. If we took them out we were afraid that the other members of the combine would exercise some damning and bankrupting influence upon the government of Canada". Just on this point I again remind the Prime Minister that the control of rates was the suggestion in the Speech from the Throne; but under this proposal of Mr. Preston, and under the proposal of the Minister of Trade and Commerce this afternoon, the objective is to smash this combine. I should like the House to bear that in mind-the intention is to smash the combine. Very good. We will find out before we get through, the feasibility of smashing it with the puny weapon that the government has taken into its hands.
Now, the letter goes on to say that there has been occasional discrimination, that freight rates have been excessive, and that the insurance on the St. Lawrence is higher, and so on. I want to examine briefly one or two of these points. In the first place it has been known for years that the insurance rates on the St. Lawrence harm been high. It does not follow that a North Atlantic combine is to blame for the insurance rates on the St. Lawrence; that fact has nothing to do with the North Atlantic conference at all. As a matter of fact this government has to its credit the lowering of insurance to some slight degree:	They added thirty days to the
end of the open season, and took fifteen days
Ocean Shipping Rates

off the first part of the season. In other words they added fifteen days to the St. Lawrence route during which favourable rates are granted. They also secured the same rates of insurance in the case of shipping from Halifax as are obtained in the case of shipping from New York. That is the way to do it. I want to say to the Prime Minister that it is by dealing with this question step by step-here a problem solved and there a problem solved-that these great commercial and trade matters are properly and effectively treated. The government, however, seem to have departed wholly from that course in regard to this as well as in regard to other matters.
Now with respect to discrimination, I wish to examine the report at feme little length. On pages 14 and 15 of the report will be found certain schedules. If the House will examine these schedules, and if the House will recall the speech of the Minister of Trade and Commerce this afternoon, it will remember and it will note this: That in every case it refers to a discrimination against British shipping from British ports, and very little in these schedules touches Canada at all. The report deals with the schedules from continental and United Kingdom ports to all sections of the world. Well, that is quite all right, but as to discrimination against British ports I want to ask in all fairness and with all courtesy, is it our business to take up the cudgels in behalf of the British shippers? Surely the British ship owners and the British merchants are wise enough, and skilled enough, and experienced enough to look after their own affairs. I do not want to say or to infer that we should wholly disregard their interests, but I do say that it is not the business of this country, of this parliament, or of this government to supply a subsidy to protect British shipping and British ports. Let us see what the British say themselves. I have it in their own reports, and it is worth reading. I wonder if the hon. member for Brome (Mr. McMaster) is in the House? Yes, I see him here. I wish he would listen to this particular clause. This is a clause drawn up by the British Commission on Shipping and Ship-building of 1918, and it must be remembered that it is drawn up by a free trade country so that there is something in it which seems to violate that idea.

subtopic: AGREEMENT WITH SIR WILLIAM PETERSEN- MOTION IN FAVOUR OF RATIFICATION
speechtext:
Sound philosophy and
good sense.

subtopic: AGREEMENT WITH SIR WILLIAM PETERSEN- MOTION IN FAVOUR OF RATIFICATION
speechtext:
My hon. friend in advance stamps the words I am about to quote as sound philosophy and good sense.

The British ship owner has to compete with the foreign ship owner in the provision of service, just as the British manufacturer has to compete with the foreign manufacturer in the supply of commodities.
That is perfectly sound. Then this report goes on to say:
To meet such competition rates for foreign goods may at times be lower than rates for British goods, just as British goods may be sold abroad at lower prices than they are sold to the home consumer.

subtopic: AGREEMENT WITH SIR WILLIAM PETERSEN- MOTION IN FAVOUR OF RATIFICATION
speechtext: Hear, hear.

subtopic: AGREEMENT WITH SIR WILLIAM PETERSEN- MOTION IN FAVOUR OF RATIFICATION
speechtext:
Good free trade doctrine. The hon. member for Brome (Mr. McMaster) has stamped this with his approval already.
Some latitude in this respect must be allowed to the
ship owner as it is allowed to the manufacturer, since international competition would otherwise be impossible.
I pause to emphasize the point. The minister comes before us with a resolution approving of a subsidy of $1,300,000 a year to certain steamship lines. What for? He says they are discriminating against British ports and British shippers to every port in the world. I will come to Canada in a minute. The British House in their own report state that such things are permissible and that it is sometimes necessary to give a preference, to give better rates to foreign goods in order to meet the competition of international trade. I want to say that that is an economic axiom that you cannot escape; you can do what you like to seek to escape it but you cannot.
If the control of freights is confined simply to certain commodities of primary importance-
I want to read this to hon. friends to my left. I am addressing them in no captious spirit, but very seriously.
-a preference will be given to the carriage of all other commodities, and the result will therefore be the exact opposite of that intended. If the control of freights is confined to particular trade routes, British tonnage will be diverted from those trade routes to others in which the freights are not controlled.
That is perfectly sound reasoning. It is infinitely more wise than anything I find in the report before the House. It simply says this:	If you control rates in certain
commodities shippers will seek to carry other lines of goods and make as much money out of them, and raise the rates to break even in their revenue; or if you have certain ports or trade routes which are under control, shipping will be inclined to abandon those routes and frequent those that are not under control. What is the next step in the reasoning? I want hon. members from the province of Nova Scotia to consider this report. They talk about using Canadian ports. You talk about reversing this practice of shipping goods from Providence, Rhode Island, Boston

Ocean Shipping Rates
and other ports but if you put a restrictive control upon Canadian routes you will find goods diverted through Maine and other states and going out through American ports. There is no escape from that. This British report, which represents a study of the whole situation, points to the danger of this form of control and restriction. We turn for a moment to Canada. We have a case where Canadian rates are higher than the rates from Germany. This is the matter upon which the writer of this report has apparently based a great deal of importance. He points out that goods coming from Hamburg to New York axe carried at a lower rate than goods from Canada to Liverpool. In this case he is comparing the rates westward to the rates eastward, a comparison which is neither fair proper, nor germane to the subject at all. That is about all the reference he makes to Canadian goods, except that I find a reference to grain, which I will deal with in a moment. The point that I wish to make at this stage is that ships from Canadian ports carry full cargoes eastward to the European ports, but almost invariably they come back with perhaps about a quarter cargo. I think that is a fair statement of the case. The result is that if you carry a full cargo one way and a quarter cargo the other way, the rates on the goods carried must be sufficient to pay for the trip both ways. That is a simple problem and a simple fact. That is one of the reasons why Canadian rates are high. Perhaps some of my hon. friends will say, "Well then, why not lower your tariff, so as to make a larger flow of goods into Canada?"

subtopic: AGREEMENT WITH SIR WILLIAM PETERSEN- MOTION IN FAVOUR OF RATIFICATION
speechtext: Hear, hear.

subtopic: AGREEMENT WITH SIR WILLIAM PETERSEN- MOTION IN FAVOUR OF RATIFICATION
speechtext: I find that I have properly interpreted the view of some. I have a remedy which I think is much better than that. If you followed that course and- lowered your tariff so as to admit goods into the country, it is not likely you would increase the amount of goods coming from Europe or Great Britain, and the chances are that you would increase the influx of goods from the United States. To remedy this situation in Canada in regard to open freight rates, we want full cargoes from Europe. Bu.t they must be made up of goods bought in England or in Europe, which are to-day bought in the United States. I will tell my hon. friends why I hold to that point.

subtopic: AGREEMENT WITH SIR WILLIAM PETERSEN- MOTION IN FAVOUR OF RATIFICATION
speechtext: We favour a British preference.

subtopic: AGREEMENT WITH SIR WILLIAM PETERSEN- MOTION IN FAVOUR OF RATIFICATION
speechtext:
I will very gladly discuss the British preference, but I want to finish
my argument if I may. I say we should increase the cargoes from Europe at the expense of the cargoes coming from the United States. I do not want to get into a side discussion, but I think the point is worth making. We owe the United States annually in interest about two hundred million dollars. In order to break even with them we ought to sell them two hundred million dollars per year more than we do. As a matter of fact we are importing annually from them two to three hundred million dollars worth of goods more than they bu3r from us, the result being that we are going behind the United States some four hundred and fifty or five hundred million dollars per year, and it is about time we designed a policy, irrespective of how we do it, that would divert to Europe and Canada the purchase of some of the goods which are now brought in from south of the line. That policy will go a long way to remedy the very grievance that we are labouring undter at the present time.
I will pass to another point, and I pause to remind the Prime Minister of something that I think perhaps he will find interesting.
I know that I found it interesting. Would he recall that in his speech delivered in this House a few weeks ago, on the occasion of the debate on the Address, he took a great deal of time to demonstrate that our foreign trade was in a splendid condition and our manufacturers better off than manufacturers south of the line and that conditions generally in Canada were more normal than conditions south of the line. I should like to read to the House what his special emissary says in that regard. In a paragraph headed "Closing down" he quotes an extract from some anonymous writer regarding that and says:
Further quotations from departmental correspondence [DOT]are uncalled for. It is only necessary to say that complaints have been received by the Department of Trade and Commerce from correspondents extending from the Maritime to the western provinces, clearly indicating that the increase in the cost of overseas transportation has played serious havoc with manufacturers, agriculturists, exporters and traders, as well as causing unemployment in industrial circles, and is also adversely affecting communities which otherwise would be fairly prosperous.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: AGREEMENT WITH SIR WILLIAM PETERSEN- MOTION IN FAVOUR OF RATIFICATION
speechtext: Hear, hear.

subtopic: AGREEMENT WITH SIR WILLIAM PETERSEN- MOTION IN FAVOUR OF RATIFICATION
speechtext:
The Prime Minister says "hear, hear". The other day my right hon. leader pointed out that there was serious havoc played in the industries and in the prosperity of the citizens of this country. The Prime Minister took three hours to try to persuade this House and the country that my right hon. leader was all wrong.
Ocean Shipping Rates

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: AGREEMENT WITH SIR WILLIAM PETERSEN- MOTION IN FAVOUR OF RATIFICATION
speechtext:
No. I said
that notwithstanding the fact that conditions were bad, they were much better in Canada in some particulars than in the United States.

subtopic: AGREEMENT WITH SIR WILLIAM PETERSEN- MOTION IN FAVOUR OF RATIFICATION
speechtext: They must be pretty bad over there.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: AGREEMENT WITH SIR WILLIAM PETERSEN- MOTION IN FAVOUR OF RATIFICATION
speechtext: They are.

subtopic: AGREEMENT WITH SIR WILLIAM PETERSEN- MOTION IN FAVOUR OF RATIFICATION
speechtext:
It is rather strange to find upon what grounds they consider our rates unfair as compared with those obtaining in the United States. If the United States have better rates than we have and their rates are bad, and this report says that these conditions are because of rates, then the rates in the United States being low must be the cause of their being in a worse condition than we are. The Prime Minister's proposals will not bear examination. He knows that quite well. He sought to imply in this House the other day, that conditions were excellent. I merely read this to show that one of his chosen henchmen differs from him in this regard.
By the way, I notice that this refers to the department of the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Low). He says that his files are filled with this sort of correspondence, and I was wondering when I read it, how the minister had the hardihood to issue that famous advertisement that Canada had turned the corner.
These schedules to which I have referred furnish the grievance which is claimed on behalf of Canada. I want to refer to the wheat situation and this is of intense interest. May I say to my hon. friends who are seriously interested in arriving at some proper solution of this problem, that wheat, flour, sugar and cattle have never been under the conference rates? They are not controlled by this alleged combine at all. They are excluded from it and are free from these rates.

subtopic: AGREEMENT WITH SIR WILLIAM PETERSEN- MOTION IN FAVOUR OF RATIFICATION
speechtext: On what authority is that statement made?

subtopic: AGREEMENT WITH SIR WILLIAM PETERSEN- MOTION IN FAVOUR OF RATIFICATION
speechtext: No one will dispute it.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: AGREEMENT WITH SIR WILLIAM PETERSEN- MOTION IN FAVOUR OF RATIFICATION
speechtext: Oh, oh.

subtopic: AGREEMENT WITH SIR WILLIAM PETERSEN- MOTION IN FAVOUR OF RATIFICATION
speechtext: Will the Minister of Justice dispute it?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: AGREEMENT WITH SIR WILLIAM PETERSEN- MOTION IN FAVOUR OF RATIFICATION
speechtext:
I am laughing at the
authority quoted by my hon. friend.

subtopic: AGREEMENT WITH SIR WILLIAM PETERSEN- MOTION IN FAVOUR OF RATIFICATION
speechtext: The Minister of Justice is, perhaps, one of those happy individuals that can see a joke in almost any tragedy, but he will not take the responsibility of saying that I am wrong in the matter.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: AGREEMENT WITH SIR WILLIAM PETERSEN- MOTION IN FAVOUR OF RATIFICATION
speechtext:
No, but the hon. member's authority seems rather poor.

Mr. STEVENS. Does it? I can give further authority.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: AGREEMENT WITH SIR WILLIAM PETERSEN- MOTION IN FAVOUR OF RATIFICATION
speechtext: All right.

subtopic: AGREEMENT WITH SIR WILLIAM PETERSEN- MOTION IN FAVOUR OF RATIFICATION
speechtext: If the minister had given me time, I would have done so, but I ask him: Will he dispute my authority, my own statement? He will not. He knows better. I ask the Minister of Trade and Commerce, his colleague: Am I right or am I wrong in asserting that wheat, flour, sugar and cattle are exempted from the conference rates? He can accept the advice of my hon. friend behind him. Not one of them will dispute it. They know perfectly well I am right. I do not see the hon. member for St. Lawrence-St. George (Mr. Marler) in his seat, but I know that he would at once confirm my statement.

subtopic: AGREEMENT WITH SIR WILLIAM PETERSEN- MOTION IN FAVOUR OF RATIFICATION
speechtext: The burden of proof rests with my hon. friend.

subtopic: AGREEMENT WITH SIR WILLIAM PETERSEN- MOTION IN FAVOUR OF RATIFICATION
speechtext:
This is delightful. Will
the Minister of Justice bear the Minister of Trade and Commerce out in that statement? I appeal to him. He is the legal authority.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: AGREEMENT WITH SIR WILLIAM PETERSEN- MOTION IN FAVOUR OF RATIFICATION
speechtext:
I certainly concur with
my colleague that he who makes an assertion must prove it.

subtopic: AGREEMENT WITH SIR WILLIAM PETERSEN- MOTION IN FAVOUR OF RATIFICATION
speechtext: I am not a lawyer, but I will venture this opinion, that the Minister of Trade and Commerce has got the cart before the horse; he has it reversed. It is not my business to prove my authorities at all. If my hon. friends dispute my authorities, it is up to them to show that I am wrong.

subtopic: AGREEMENT WITH SIR WILLIAM PETERSEN- MOTION IN FAVOUR OF RATIFICATION
speechtext: Oh, oh.

subtopic: AGREEMENT WITH SIR WILLIAM PETERSEN- MOTION IN FAVOUR OF RATIFICATION
speechtext:
There goes the Minister
of Agriculture with a laugh.

subtopic: AGREEMENT WITH SIR WILLIAM PETERSEN- MOTION IN FAVOUR OF RATIFICATION
speechtext: I never heard such a doctrine in my life.

subtopic: AGREEMENT WITH SIR WILLIAM PETERSEN- MOTION IN FAVOUR OF RATIFICATION
speechtext: I repeat that wheat, flour, sugar and cattle are not, and never have been, included in the conference rates. I state further that I have this from shipping authorities both in Montreal and in other sections. I am not going to go any further in regard to quotations.

subtopic: AGREEMENT WITH SIR WILLIAM PETERSEN- MOTION IN FAVOUR OF RATIFICATION
speechtext: As a matter of information, would the hon. gentleman tell me if there are any fixed rates with regard to the commodities which he has just mentioned?

subtopic: AGREEMENT WITH SIR WILLIAM PETERSEN- MOTION IN FAVOUR OF RATIFICATION
speechtext: No.

subtopic: AGREEMENT WITH SIR WILLIAM PETERSEN- MOTION IN FAVOUR OF RATIFICATION
speechtext: There is competition?

subtopic: AGREEMENT WITH SIR WILLIAM PETERSEN- MOTION IN FAVOUR OF RATIFICATION
speechtext:
Certainly there is.

Ocean Shipping Rates

subtopic: AGREEMENT WITH SIR WILLIAM PETERSEN- MOTION IN FAVOUR OF RATIFICATION
speechtext:
Will the hon. gentleman
quote his authority for that?

subtopic: AGREEMENT WITH SIR WILLIAM PETERSEN- MOTION IN FAVOUR OF RATIFICATION
speechtext:
Yes-myself. I am going to give my hon. friends some facts in connection with the matter. In 1923, from Montreal, there were 200 tramp steamers and 598 line steamers. The tramp steamers carried 48,600,000 bushels of wheat or 42 per cent, and the line steamers carried 65,000,000 bushels of wheat or 58 per cent. In 1924, there were 367 tramp steamers and 570 line steamers. The tramp steamers carried 94,700,000 bushels of wheat or 62 per cent, and the line steamers carried 57,600,000 bushels or 38 per cent. My figures will be slightly different from those of some of the shipping interests of Montreal, because my figures are the harbour board figures. There may be a slight variation, which is accounted for in this way, that the shipping bodies, in their report, deal with the exact amount that was handled out as of certain dates, while the harbour board may deal with slightly different dates. This may make a difference of a few bushels, but the difference is so slight that it is not worth mentioning.
As regards cattle, in 1923, there were 28,966 shipped and in 1924, 41,892. If my hon. friends want my authority, I have in my hand in regard to both of these items,
9 p.m. the customs reports which I secured from the Customs department presided over by the hon. member for Three Rivers (Mr. Bureau). This is the authority I am quoting. I am not going further into details, but what I want to make perfectly clear is this: First, no one will question this, that tramp steamers are not members of the combine. The tramp steamers from the port of Montreal carried 62 per cent of the wheat. Giving my hon. friends, for the moment, the pleasure, if they like, of questioning my authority regarding the wheat being outside of conference rates, at least the quantity of
94,700,000	bushels carried by tramp steamers last year was outside of the conference rates. They must admit that, although they would not admit the other. The point I want to make is that about one-half of this wheat- the quantity varies from year to year; sometimes it is more, sometimes less-is American wheat brought in early in the season through the port of Montreal, and it is, perhaps, the most valuable freight carried by the Canadian National and the Canadian Pacific, but more by the Canadian National than the Canadian Pacific. Does the government propose to subsidize to the extent of $1,300,000
a year Petersen steamers to carry American grain to Great Britain?

subtopic: AGREEMENT WITH SIR WILLIAM PETERSEN- MOTION IN FAVOUR OF RATIFICATION

I will answer

subtopic: AGREEMENT WITH SIR WILLIAM PETERSEN- MOTION IN FAVOUR OF RATIFICATION

speechtext:
Here is a dealer in
Montreal, say, who buys a lot of wheat stored in one of the elevators there. That wheat is partly American and partly Canadian wheat,

and he owns it. Is the government going to say that this particular man shall have the special low rate and that this other man shall not have it? After all, we put our finger on the very crux of the whole business, the absurdity of it, when we deal with this point. And let the, Prime Minister bear in mind that ten ships will make no great impress on the traffic out of Montreal alone, to say nothing of Halifax, St. John, Quebec, Vancouver, Victoria and Prince Rupert.

speechtext:
I take my right hon.
friend's word for that, and we shall "wait and sea". And that is another point which I may touch upon. This arrangement is so elastic that the government may extend the number of ships to a hundred and may spend $10,000,000 a year in the enterprise. The Prime Minister nods his head, and that is precisely the danger of the whole thing; at the whim of a minister this agreement may be enlarged until it obligates the country in tremendous sums. And what for? To benefit some designated shipper, to favour some particular port or route, and in consequence to involve this country in endless discord between shipper and ship owner.

speechtext:
We shall see what the
House wishes, and we will take care that the House is given an opportunity to express

its views on the matter. I turn now to the question of immigration, in regard to which the report has much to say. It declares that the charges for immigrants have been greatly increased, and I admit that. It may be that the charges for immigrants at the present time are unreasonable; I am not disputing that point. But I would point this out. I have seen immigrant ships come to this country for twenty-five or thirty years and I know what the accommodation on the present liners to-day is, and in the light of my experience I want to tell the House that there is no comparison between the state of affairs now and what it was at that time. As everyone knows, it is impossible to expect immigrants to come to Canada to-day under the conditions that prevailed twenty-five or thirty years ago, when immigrants were housed like cattle. In the second place, the costs have risen. Whether or not they have so risen as to justify the present rate, I am not in a position to say, but I do assert that it is unfair to suggest that immigrants can be carried at the rates that were charged twenty-five years ago. But this point is more important still: the rates that obtained say twenty years ago applied at a time when there were literally millions of immigrants coming across the Atlantic. Let me give the figures. In 1913 there came to Canada 303,000 immigrants as compared with 108,000 in 1924, while the figures show that in 1913 there came to the United States 1,079,000 as against 395,000 in 1924. In other words, the United States, by an act of congress placing a limitation upon the number of immigrants that may be admitted to that country, has restricted immigration to such an extent that it is now less than a third of what it was twelve years ago. And Canada by its process of selected immigration, with which policy, generally speaking, I wholly agree, has confined its immigration to about one-third of what it was in 1913. And you cannot expect the same rates to be charged to-day when the traffic is only one-third of what it was formerly.
Now I come to the question of the remedy which the government proposes. The government proposes ten ships, and I would ask hon. gentlemen to bear in mind that from Montreal last year there sailed out nine hundred and thirteen vessels, while from Vancouver there were over a thousand, so that these two ports account for over two thousand vessels. And the government intends putting on ten ships, which probably will make about fifty or sixty trips in the year. Is it reasonable to expect any serious impress to be made on the shipping of the country by such a service as this, when we reflect that two ports

alone account for some two thousand vessels? And in addition to that, consider Halifax, St. John, Quebec, Victoria and Prince Rupert. It seems to me that any proposal of this kind, if it is to be effective, must apply to all ports in Canada alike, and at the present time this is limited to Atlantic ports.
I apprehend that someone may question me and I had better state my authority; the Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe) may insist upon that. In paragraph 4 of the preamble to the agreement I find that the government has thought it wise to adopt such means as may be deemed expedient and necessary to "such supervision and control of trans-Atlantic freight rates", and so on.
Why should the government abandon the Pacific coast when we are told in the report that the combine is world-wide and covers every sea and trade route? Why, the picture drawn by Preston is one that would wring the heart of any credulous person who did not know who the author was. But if this combine is world-wide, why should not the government apply the agreement to Pacific as well as to Atlantic ports? Why limit the agreement to the Atlantic? And I emphasize once again the fact that ten vessels applied even to the one port of Montreal will prove inadequate. The Prime Minister a moment ago referred to the character of the ships. I have a brief comparison to make and I invite his consideration to it. In the first place, in the schedule covering the type of vessels contemplated, I find that the particulars are "without guarantee." Do the Prime Minister and his government realize what that means? The Prime Minister says that nothing can be changed ; this agreement stands as it is. Well, if it stands as it is, these specifications of the ships are without guarantee, and there is no reason in the world why Petersen should not vary them one way or the other at his whim and fancy. Let me compare them briefly with the present Canadian Government Merchant Marine ships. The Petersen ships, "without guarantee," have a gross tonnage of 5,000 while the merchant marine vessels, twenty-five ships, of the 8,100 ton class, have a gross tonnage of 5,751. The net tonnage of the Petersen ships is 3,500; of the Canadian Government Merchant Marine 3.550. And, by the way, net tonnage is the test. The speed of the Petersen ships [DOT]-unguaranteed, mark you-is 11 knots; the speed of the Canadian Government Merchant Marine ships on a six-mile trial trip was HI knots. Repairs to the Petersen ships, I am informed by men thoroughly competent to advise in the matter, owing to the unique construction of their internal combustion en-
Ocean Shi-pping Rates
gines can only be made in Great Britain in virtually the one place where they are now built; that is, the cylinders of these engines are made of a peculiar steel that is not kept in stock in other yards. Consequently these ships will find great difficulty in securing engine repairs on this side of the water. The Canadian Government Merchant Marine ships are more or less of a standard type and therefore can be repaired in any port throughout the world. A great deal of stress is laid upon the value of internal combustion engines because of the saving in fuel. But it is well to bear in mind that owing to the fluctuating price of fuel oil many oil-burning ships today are being converted back into coal burners.
I am not speaking of the fast passenger ships, but of this class of cargo boat. The Petersen ships will have a grain capacity of 580,000 cubic feet as against 447,000 cubic feet of the 8,500 ton Canadian Government Merchant Marine boats; but the difference is not very great, and as regards our 10,000 ton ships the capacity is about the same as that of the Petersen ships.
Now let me deal briefly with the cost of this proposal. A ten-year period with principal and interest amounts to an expenditure of over $17,000,000; a 20-year period, with principal and interest compounded, amounts to $46,200,000. The government are asking us virtually to commit the country to an expenditure of some $17,000,000 over a period of ten years. But the Prime Minister says that if he and his colleagues think the contract is working out successfully they may extend it indefinitely; at any rate, there is no limit in the agreement. What are we asked to do this for? For the alleged purpose of smashing, as the Minister of Trade and Commerce says, the North Atlantic combine. This measure will plunge the country into excessive expense. This is no time for us to indulge in experiments that will cost the taxpayers large sums of money. Infinitely better would it be to apply this sum annually to debt reduction, although it may be a small sum in comparison with the national debt, rather than waste it in an abortive effort to control ocean freight rates in this manner.
The Preston report upon which the government rests its case is prejudiced and unfair, and bears all the earmarks of an effusion from a narrow and jaundiced mind; nor does any utterance upon any subject by this author carry any conviction or respect in this country. This may sound a little harsh, but I want to say it very frankly. Certain men may be very clever, they may be useful in elections to pull their party out of a difficult corner,

And what happens? Here is the penalty clause, Mr. Speaker, that this lawyer, whom the minister referred to as the greatest lawyer in Canada-and we will find out later who it is-has inserted in the contract:
If at any time after the expiration of the eighteen months mentioned in paragraph 1 (c) the contractor should fail to carry on the said service with the full complement of ten ships, the minister may by notice in writing call upon him to supply the deficiency within a delay of three months, and in default of the contractor's doing so within such delay, the minister may terminate the contract by notice in writing.
When Mr. Petersen aJbandons his contract and leaves us high and dry, I picture the

The man having already abandoned the contract is under no penalty whatever! In the meantime we have been paying him diuring the period of the experiment, $1,300,000 a year, and at the same time we have disturbed and upset our trade arrangements and our shipping connections, and we have driven every tramp steamer out of the business.
Now, if the House will pardon me a little humour after so much seriousness. The Minister of Trade of Commerce and his friend the author of this report, remind me of the story of two Irishmen-

Now for my story. There were two Irishmen, the story goes who met a bob-tailed wildcat and chased it for a while, and finally drove it up a tree. Mike sent Pat up to shake it down. Pat shakes it down, and Mike catches it. Pat shouts down, "Have you the wildcat?" "Yes," cries Mike "but come down and help me let it go." subtopic: AGREEMENT WITH SIR WILLIAM PETERSEN- MOTION IN FAVOUR OF RATIFICATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it perhaps may be fitting as I had the great honour of being chairman of the committee that looked into the matter of ocean freight rates some two years ago, if I detain the House for a little while in consideration of the matter which is now before us.
The speaker who has just resumed his seat (Mr. Stevens) stated that he did not take our report in perfect faith. In making that statement he reflected to a certain degree on certain very honourable and distinguished members of his own party, because the two reports which were brought into the House by this committee on ocean freight rates were unanimous reports, concurred in by the former Minister of Agriculture in the government of my right hon. friend who now leads the opposition, concurred in by a gentleman of the Conservative party who at one time, I understand, occupied the important position of Minister of Agriculture in the province of Ontario, and by two other distinguished and hon. members of this House; and in reflecting upon the report the hon. member for Vancouver Centre (Mr. Stevens) was reflecting upon the wisdom or patriotism of these gentlemen as well as upon the wisdom or patriotism of other members of the committee. I would be prepared to leave the appreciation of the conduct of our committee and of the actions of the chairman in regard thereto in the hands of my fellow members of that committee who belong to the Conservative persuasion. There was not from the beginning the slightest attempt to make political capital out of the matters which came before us for investigation. I would gladly bear testimony to the work which all the members performed on that committee. We worked literally night and day in endeavouring to get at the facts, and with no other endeavour, and when we had got some of the facts concerning certain phases of our inquiry-our time was not sufficient to enable us to go fully into all the multitudinous matters brought before us,-we made two reports on the question of ocean freight rates. Those reports were concurred in unanimously by all the members of the committee; they were concurred in without cavil by all the members of this House.
Now the gentleman who has just taken his seat does not state that there is not a North 47

Atlantic conference or combine, but he rather objects to the word combine; he prefers the word conference, and though he does not exactly praise it, he would give us to understand that this combination of shipping interests is really rather beneficial than otherwise. It is true that it may require some slight correction here and there, but according to him, its virtues far outweigh its vices. Here again he falls foul, I will not say of a more distinguished member of the party which sits in the comer immediately at your left, Mr. Speaker, but he falls foul of the gentleman who occupied in a previous administration the very honourable and onerous position of Minister of Finance, a gentleman who in earlier, I will not say happier days, was the chairman of the Board of Railway Commissioners for Canada, and who looked into this matter and reported upon it to the government of the day; and his view of the situation was precisely the same view to which this committee arrived at.
I could not expect the House to listen with patience to me if I went over all our report, but perhaps I may be permitted to draw the attention of the House to certain of its salient features. We brought in two reports, one on the 23rd of April1, 1923, and one on the 18th of June, 1923. In our first report we set forth that there was a combine, that there was a North Atlantic and U.K. Conference Eastward-Bound-I think that is the full title of the organization-which met every month in New York and there agreed on certain rates, and that there was also a committee of various lines trading out of Montreal called the Weekly Liner Committee. The matter in which the Liner Committee operated was as follows-I read from our report:
The general rates were set at the North Atlantic and U.K. Conference in New York, but for the purpose of united action in regard to these and other rates, a weekly meeting was held, at which representatives of all the steamship lines attended. At this meeting, rates were agreed upon, and no member of the line had the right to depart from the rates so established without conferring with, and warning his competitors of his intention so to do. An earnestly worded expostulation would be directed by one member to another if this line of conduct was not followed.
Theu we pointed out in our report that the operation of this conference had brought about this most extraordinary result:
The government of the United States forced the Shipping board, which manages the United States governmentally-owned steamers, to make a very low rate for the transportation of flour to Europe, a rate stated by the shipping companies to be below a commercial rate. This rate applied only to flour ground in the United States. To meet this rate, the North Atlantic Conference lines established at a given'moment a rate of 15 cents per 100 pounds on flour ground in the
Ocean Shipping Rates

United States, while they maintained a rate of 19 cents per 100 pounds on Canadian flour-a very substantial differential against our Canadian millers.
That rather disposes of the appeal made by the hon. member for Vanoouver Centre (Mr. Stevens) that flour was always free, that flour was never controlled by the conference. As a matter of fact, the hon. member was mistaken in that regard.
In our second report we dealt somewhat thoroughly with the history, not of the shipping rings, but with the history of the investigations which had been made into the shipping rings. We examined with care the report made by the Royal Commission on Shipping Rings in 1909; that is the report to which the hon. member for Vancouver Centre has referred in his somewhat extended remarks. But what he drew the attention of the House to was the report of the majority of the committee, and this majority was made up largely of men who were not unconnected with the shipping business. They therefore gave to themselves a very high certificate of character. But the members of that committee who were less intimately connected with the shipping rings were somewhat more critical and the labour member of the committee, a gentleman by the name of Madison, made a very strong reservation and came out whole heartedly with the view that shipping combines were on the whole evil and not good things. I think we were very fair in our report in this matter. We gave a succinct and I think a fair account of the findings of all three classes of commissioners who subscribed to that report. We gave the findings of the majority of the commissioners and even the majority who investigated into the shipping rings were not satisfied with the way things were going on. Their solution was that groups of shippers should combine in associations that could face the powerful shipping ring: that one group should be organized to "faire face," as we say in the language of the province of Quebec, to present a united front against the association of the ship owners. But we also brought before the House the findings of the minority of the commiisioners. Now, the minority of the commissioners found along lines which I think tend to appeal to the sen.-ie of the people of this country. It certainly appealed to the sense of the hon. member for West York (Sir Henry Drayton) when he looked into the matter. This is what the minority of the commissioners saad:
All monopolies are liable to abuse, to a greater or less extent, unless they are strictly limited either by nature of the case, by legislation, or by some form of supervision.

And again:
There is. of course, a presumption against a monopoly in any branch of trade being beneficial to the community.
Again:
The benefits of the organization which they (toe
shipping companies) adopt for the purposes of their business must be valued, mainly with reference to its effect, not on the shipping companies, but on the general public.
I should not like to detain the House in setting forth all the conclusions to which this minority came, but I may be allowed to draw attention to a few of them. I suppose we are all agreed that it is a good thing to have cheap freight rates either on land or on water. But freight rates should not be driven down to such an extent, either on land or on water, that there is not a fair and reasonable return for the capital invested. I think that is reasonable, I think that is fair, unless there is too much capital invested, in which case it might be quite proper that rates should be driven down until the capital in the industry represents fairly the earnings earned upon it. But with that proviso I think I am within the sense, the common sense of this House, that we are all on common ground in saying that with provision for a proper return for capital it is paramount under our present economic system that goods should move freely from place to place, and that freight rates should be brought down to what would be a fair return for the public service rendered. That being the case I think we will all agree with the statement that:
The system was introduced in the first instance with the object of raising rates or preventing their fall and diminishing competition
It has been successful in raising or keeping up rates;
The public have as a rule, to pay higher rates of freight than they would pay in an open market;
The system has been injurious to "tramps", the strongest element in the British Mercantile marine, and it leads as to them to waste and to higher rates of freight.
The system tends to waste in various other directions owing to the manner in which the rings are constituted;
There is no satisfactory evidence that the saving in cost, if there be any. under the system of shipping rings, exceeds the waste which is due to that system;
The system tends to inflate the amount of tonnage and consequently the amount of capital invested upon which interest has to be paid.
I think that is merely an example of an economic law which is of almost universal application, namely-that if you artificially- whether by restriction of competition, or otherwise-increase for the time being the reward of capital in any certain given line you will induce more capital to flow into that line; that therefore you will produce an excess of capital in that line; that excess of capital will aim to earn money for itself; that rates

Ocean Shipping Rates
and prices will increase, and in the long run the business which it affected will be hurt and that capital which has entered into that artificially stimulated channel will be hurt as well. It seems to me a grateful thing to listen to the energetic and eloquent paean of praise in favour of an absence of artificiality put forth this evening by the hon. member for Vancouver Centre. I would invite him to follow that wholesome line of reasoning into many other spheres of social, political and economic thought.
After dealing with this long report on shipping rings we dealt with the report made in 1913 by the hon. member for West York (Sir Henry Drayton) who was then chairman of the Board of Railway Commissioners. His findings were practically the findings of the minority who had examined into the shipping rates. I will not say that he found in his report everything that they found, but I think that the conclusions which he arrived at were based, in large measure, upon the same reasonings and he came very much to the same conclusion that they did. I know that we based ours, in making our report, in no small measure upon the findings of a commissioner who went over there with judicial experience for the purpose of finding out the facts without, I may say, the slightest inclination to veer either to the right or to the left, and I think that it is a complete answer to those who would depend too strongly upon the favourable findings of this British commission if I might quote the words used by the hon. member for West York when he said in his report "Notwithstanding the information which I received from the conference lines, I am still of the view that an investigation should be held".
I am at one with the hon. member for Vancouver Centre when he says this matter is of the greatest difficulty and that it behooves us all to get at the real facts of the case. I cannot imagine a wiser step than that intimated by the Minister of Trade and Commerce this afternoon that this resolution shall be placed before a special committee of this House for investigation into the matter, and that before this committee there will be opportunities given for all interested parties to make their representations known.
May I just say that this should not be a matter upon which men should differ on party lines. I cannot see that there should be any difference of opinion between patriotic Canadian citizens as to the advisability of getting the cheapest freight rates that we can and all the facts we possibly can in order that our 47 V
ways may be guided wisely and justly in the matter.
In our report we dealt with the finding of the Dominions Royal Commission which has been referred to by the minister in his address to the House this afternoon, and we also drew the attention of the House to the fact that there had been a similar movement in the United States, a similar attempt made to control freight rates by that country, and that the great publicist Lubin who founded the great Institute of Agriculture at Rome, had given us his opinion that it was vital for the agricultural interests of the world that some international body should control freight rates on the seas, because the question was in effect international and) not national. Mr. Lubin in his report to congress shows how those who control the freight rates of the world control the supply of the staple commodities of the world, and how, if they are in league with speculators they may mulct not only the consumer but also the producer. That is one of the matters that we dealt with in our report, and I feel that that report, in view of the unanimity in which it was prepared, offered and accepted, might be accorded full faith and credit, even by leading members of the party which sits immediately to the left of the Speaker.
I have dealt at some length with the report itself, and I will now proceed to answer a few of the arguments which were advanced by the hon. member for Vancouver Centre (Mr. Stevens). The statement was made that the concern of British shippers was not our concern. and that British shippers might well be left to look after themselves. If that statement had been made by a nationalist of the province of Quebec I know what the Toronto Telegram would have said the next morning. What was the object of this country some time ago in giving a preference to British goods but to encourage trade between ourselves and the British Isles, I could not help remarking with a certain amount of interest-and my hon. friend will pardon me if I say also amusement-the emphatic statement made that if return cargoes could not be obtained freight rates must be paid both ways on any shipment. The hon. leader of the Progressive party (Mr. Forke) interjected' a question as to how that attitude of mind comported with the desire expressed in some influential quarters to get rid of the British preference; but when that question was suggested my hon. friend wisely gave silence for a reply.
It seems to me that perhaps a few words may be spoken concerning the arguments used by the hon. member for Vancouver Centre
Ocean Shipping Rates

that what we must do is to devise a policy which will divert trade from its natural channel and into unnatural channels. That was in effect his argument when he pointed out that we had what he would be pleased to call an adverse balance of trade with the United States, and that we should endeavour by legislation to change that adverse balance of trade. Now, Mr. Speaker, we do not buy anything from the United States unless we can get better value for our money by so doing. We buy nothing from Great Britain, Germany, Austria or Italy unless those who are charged with the purchase of it think they can get the best value for their money. It is preposterous nonsense-and I say it in all kindness-to think you can effectively divert trade from its natural channels by legislation. Let me give the House an example which I gleaned from the pages of the report of the Economic conference which was attended by the Prime Minister and the Minister of Railways the autumn before last. The representative of India said that after the war they had endeavoured to direct their trade in raw hides from Germany to Great Britain. They had apparently in India-at least so I gathered from the report-a large trade in light hides, and prior to the war these light hides had been going largely to Germany. They had an export duty on these hides of 15 per cent. They cut the duty to Great Britain down to 10 per cent, and maintained the 15 per cent duty on hides sent to Germany; but the hides went to Germany just the same. Why? Because that was the natural place for them to go, because trade had worn that channel, because, as the representative from India said, the German people seemed to be the only people who were able as a good business venture, to work up or deal in these light hides. We had at the time when the National Policy was introduced into this country a very much smaller trade with the United States, relatively to the trade with England than we have to-dlay; but with the introduction of the National Policy, which was supported by the slogan 'Reciprocity in trade or reciprocity in tariff," we found that relatively to our trade with Great Britain our trade with the United States increased. After 1896 we gave a large preference to British goods, but our trade with the United States increased proportionately faster than did our trade with Great Britain. In 1911 we were given an opportunity, which may not come again for many- years, the responsibility for the rejection of which will have to be borne as a crushing burden on the shoulders of the distinguished members who sit on the immediate left of the Speaker.

But even after that rejection, trade with the United States relatively kept increasing and increasing. It is folly to fight against eoonomic law and the facts of geography, and the sooner the country realizes that, and instead of trying to fight against economic law and to fight against geography, tries to take advantage of economic law and to take advantage of geography, the sooner we will arrive at a prosperous position.
In his remarks dealing with the report of this special committee investigating agricultural conditions, the member for Vancouver Centre made this statement:
Wheat, flour, cattle and sugar were never affected by the conference rate whatever.
I have not had time to look up sugar, and I am prepared for the purpose of the argument to grant that my hon. friend is right about sugar, but he is wrong about the three other commodities.

Will the hon. gentleman
allow me to interrupt?
Yes.

The hon. member is not
quite right. I said that these articles were not now and had not been for some time affected by the conference rates. They were at one time, because I am quite aware of the fact that the United States government interfered in regard to flour, so that my hon. friend is quite right in regard to that.

Perhaps my hon. friend is not quite so wrong as I thought he was. I did not understand him to say that it was merely at the present time that these were not affected by the conference rates. I do not know whether they are now affected by the conference rates, but I know that after the representatives of the lines in Montreal had endeavoured to hide from your committee the existence of their combination and combine, and that after we examined into the matter, investigated and cross-questioned them, we found out these facts and, perhaps, if they had conference rates on wheat, flour and cattle, in the past, it is quite possible that even if they do not have them on these articles now, they may easily have them in the future.
In connection, however, with cattle, there is not much room for difference of opinion, because I hold in my hand a reply of the steamship lines engaged in the Canadian north Atlantic trade to a report made by Mr. Preston, and on page 21, I read as follows:
During 1921 cattle were being shipped to continental
ports at rates varying from $75 up to $100 per head whereas conference lines were only charging $40 to the

United Kingdom during the same period, and during the same year this rate was reduced to $30 and was subsequently reduced to the present basis of $20 on cattle weighing over 1,000 pounds, and $18 for cattle weighing 1,000 pounds or under.
This is not the rate of one particular line. This is the rate stated by all the lines to *which the rates apply, and I think it is fair to say that that is a conference rate on cattle at the present time.
Let us look at the question of flour, because quite an eloquent appeal was made for support of the attitude 'assumed by my bon. friend, which after all, was an attitude rather of criticism than of constructive statesmanship, to members who sit immediately opposite me, because wheat and flour had not been controlled by conference rates. I have in my hand the evidence which was taken before the special committee on Agricultural Conditions. In part 1, at page 143 I read as follows:

Grain rates:-The lines present agreed to maintain a rate of forty cents per 100 pounds on rye, corn, barley and wheat when the latter is released, with fifty cents per 100 pounds on oats, with the exception

That applies to wheat rather than, to flour, but I may as well deal with wheat now, and there is plenty of evidence in the testimony given by these gentlemen that there was at that time and had been previously a conference rate on wheat as well as on flour.
There was also a rate on a great number of other agricultural commodities:
